video_title: From Voice Agents to AI Avatars
gist: Alex Mhola, co-founder and CEO of Bosan AI, argues that real-time voice AI is fundamentally a cost-per-conversation problem rather than a pure intelligence problem, and that his team deliberately optimized for price first — claiming benchmark parity-or-better versus GPT, Gemini and Grok at roughly one-tenth the cost with thinking disabled. He details the token-rate-versus-parameter-count tradeoff that governs voice economics, a ~100 million hour proprietary audio corpus stored in an owned data center, and a two-stage architecture where a conversational front end fires background tool/MCP calls while stalling naturally. He predicts audio becomes 'pretty much bulletproof' in about a year and audiovisual avatars — including animated faces on robots — start appearing in roughly a year to eighteen months, with voice being only an intermediate stepping stone toward them.

insights.claim: Bosan AI targets interruption handling within roughly 150 milliseconds because that is approximately the biological latency from a photon hitting the retina to the cortex processing it, making it the natural bar for feeling responsive to a human.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Gives an objective, falsifiable latency spec to benchmark any voice-agent vendor against: sub-150ms barge-in, not just fast first-token time.
insights.quote: it takes about 150 milliseconds for you know basically a photon hitting your retina to your cortex actually doing something with it

insights.claim: Human audiovisual perception effectively operates at only about 6 to 10 hertz, which caps how much temporal fidelity a real-time conversational model actually needs to deliver regardless of display refresh rates.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Sets a ceiling on useful spend: vendors paying for fidelity above human perceptual limits are burning compute margin for no user-detectable gain.
insights.quote: humans kind of operate at around maybe 6 to 10 hertz really when it comes to audio visual perception

insights.claim: Single-microphone capture will never solve multi-speaker noise cancellation for voice agents; microphone arrays are required, which pushes a meaningful share of voice-AI quality onto device hardware and OS-level audio stacks rather than the model.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Voice-agent performance is partly captured by device makers; model vendors without a strong hardware partner face a quality ceiling in real-world noisy deployments.
insights.quote: having a single microphone will probably never really solve this. You need microphone arrays to really do proper noise cancellation

insights.claim: In a noisy bar in Jeju, South Korea during the KDD conference, Bosan AI's model handled live speaker switching into Slovenian and then Hindi, with the guest crediting a non-trivial share of that success to the iOS device's noise cancellation and audio separation rather than the model alone.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Real-world multilingual robustness is now demoable outside lab conditions, but attribution between model and device stack matters when evaluating vendor claims.

insights.claim: Current consumer flagship voice interfaces such as ChatGPT advanced voice mode and the newer Codex voice remain brittle, working reliably only in silent rooms and requiring users to be unnaturally conscientious about interrupting.
insights.speaker: Sam Charrington (host)
insights.so_what: The perceived leader's voice UX is still an open competitive gap, leaving room for specialist audio-model vendors to win on naturalness.
insights.quote: It's it's very brittle, I think.

insights.claim: Even as voice improves, text input remains preferable for precision technical work such as entering serial numbers or URLs, implying voice agents will win in advisory and ambient contexts rather than displacing typing in high-precision workflows.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Bounds the addressable market for voice agents: consumer/advisory and mobile-first use cases, not precision enterprise data entry.

insights.claim: Voice models face a hard dilemma where high audio fidelity requires a high token frequency, and a high token frequency forces the model to have fewer parameters because both prefill and generation costs scale with tokens per second.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Explains why voice-native models will stay structurally smaller than frontier text models, and why 'just scale it' is not available as a strategy in this segment.
insights.quote: many tokens per second means your model cannot have too many parameters

insights.claim: Text is the ultimate compressed format at roughly three to five tokens per second for human consumption, while audio easily requires ten-plus tokens per second, so a 10-token-per-second audio stream gives each token about 100 milliseconds of temporal granularity.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: A concrete multiplier for modeling inference cost of voice versus text products: roughly 2-3x the token throughput per second of conversation.

insights.claim: Building voice AI cannot be split cleanly into engineering problems and research problems; biology, user experience, cost engineering and model science must be solved simultaneously as a single systems challenge.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Predicts that teams organized as separate research and platform orgs underperform in voice; look for vertically integrated teams when assessing competitors.

insights.claim: Avatar video generation is far cheaper than general video generation because an avatar feed is intrinsically low-motion and predictable, so models like WAN or Flux that produce ten-second clips must be modified for hour-long visually consistent streams and can then be heavily optimized.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Avatar economics decouple from general text-to-video economics, so avatar deployment could arrive well before general video generation becomes affordable.

insights.claim: The guest expects diffusion to enter audio modeling not as a replacement for sequential models but as speculative decoding paired with traditional sequential models for the overall statistical modeling.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: A watch-item for architecture shifts in real-time audio: hybrid diffusion-plus-autoregressive decoding rather than a wholesale diffusion transition.

insights.claim: Bosan AI claims it beats GPT, Gemini and Grok on audio benchmarks including Big Bench Audio and Complex Function Bench at a fraction of the cost, specifically claiming better-than-OpenAI performance at one-tenth the cost.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: If verifiable, a 10x cost advantage in conversational audio is the kind of gap that resets enterprise vendor selection in voice deployments.
insights.quote: So right now on benchmarks we are better than let's say GPT and Gemini and and and Groc at a fraction of the cost. So we're better than open eyes models at onetenth the cost.

insights.claim: The benchmark comparison Bosan AI cites is run with thinking turned off in the competing models, because visible reasoning pauses break conversational naturalness in voice.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: An important caveat for anyone underwriting the 10x claim — the comparison is set in the no-reasoning regime that voice actually requires, not peak model capability.
insights.quote: the little footnote is this is with thinking turned off in these models

insights.claim: If a real-time conversation requires a full Blackwell server GPU per single user session, the business model is not economically viable no matter how good the demo looks.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: A practical screen for voice-AI startups: ask GPU-per-concurrent-conversation, not demo quality, before assuming gross margin exists.
insights.quote: if you need to use let's say you know a full blackwell server GPU just for a single conversation then that may not be the most economically viable model

insights.claim: Bosan AI explicitly designed backwards from a target price rather than forward from maximum capability, which the guest frames as a deliberately contrarian bet against trillion-parameter 'trophy models' built to do chitchat.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: A differentiated strategic posture in a market where most capital is chasing scale; the winner in voice may be decided on unit economics rather than capability.
insights.quote: we went in with a price first and then work backwards to, you know, how can you build something that actually people can afford

insights.claim: Building a hundreds-of-billions-parameter front-end audio model produces impressive demos but uneconomic deployment, so the guest treats demo-driven architecture choices as a trap that customers ultimately pay for through the GPU bill.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Suggests a coming divergence between demo leaders and deployment leaders in voice AI — useful for timing enterprise vendor bets.
insights.quote: this this is really I think where we we we took a slightly contrarian approach where we went for affordability first

themes.theme: Audio data moat and storage cost

insights.claim: Bosan AI's primary claimed moat is its audio training corpus of roughly 100 million hours — equivalent to about 200 human lifetimes of ambient audio — sourced by scraping and crawling the internet rather than buying annotation.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete scale bar for audio-model challengers and signals that data pipeline engineering, not annotation spend, is the competitive axis.
insights.quote: So we have in the order of 100 million hours of audio. Um and it's about 200 human lifetimes.

insights.claim: Owning its own data center rather than renting from a NeoCloud or one of the big three hyperscalers is what made Bosan AI's audio-scale storage economically survivable, with the guest saying hyperscaler pricing would have been even more problematic.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Storage economics, not just GPU access, can decide whether a data-heavy AI company is viable — a reason some AI startups vertically integrate infrastructure.
insights.quote: If you were to store this data on a NeoCloud, um the storage bill would eat you alive.

insights.claim: Hard drive prices are now roughly three times what they were a year ago, forcing data-heavy AI teams that previously enjoyed cheap storage to become more prudent about retention.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: A 3x HDD price move is a real input-cost signal for storage suppliers and a margin headwind for data-hoarding AI companies.
insights.quote: by now the hard drives are about three times the price of what they were a year ago

insights.claim: Bosan AI declines vendor offers to annotate 10,000 hours of audio because its corpus is roughly 10,000 times that scale, implying the human audio-annotation services market is structurally irrelevant to frontier audio model builders.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Bearish signal for human-annotation service providers in audio; the value migrates to automated pipeline engineering instead.
insights.quote: We are at between 10 we're at 10,000 times that scale.

insights.claim: Noisy internet-scraped audio labels are workable because unbiased noisy measurements average out — the guest invokes robust regression and trimmed-mean estimators as half-a-millennium-old techniques — but the approach fails entirely if the labeling tool is biased rather than merely noisy.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Identifies bias, not noise, as the real failure mode in scraped-data training — a diligence question for any data-moat claim.

insights.claim: Context and privileged side information dramatically improve automatic audio annotation — knowing a podcast has exactly two speakers makes speaker separation easy and yields large volumes of clean single-speaker audio, mirroring the face-recognition trick of using same-actor frames across a movie.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Shows the data flywheel is built from classical ML tricks applied at scale, meaning compute and storage investment — not novel research — is the barrier to entry.

insights.claim: Bosan AI deliberately avoided building its own LLM, instead borrowing the reasoning intelligence already baked into high-quality language models and teaching them one extra modality — audio — following the same pattern as vision-language models, robotics and world models.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Confirms open-weight text models as a subsidized input layer for modality specialists — a structural reason the modality layer can stay capital-light.
insights.quote: if somebody gives you free steel, you don't build a steel mill, you build a car

insights.claim: Adding audio to an LLM without care causes catastrophic forgetting of prior reasoning and language ability, so a full pre-, mid- and post-training pipeline for text must be maintained alongside the audio pipeline, with tasks designed to ground audio and text into each other.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Explains why 'just bolt audio on a base model' startups underdeliver on intelligence, and why the real cost of a voice model is closer to that of a full LLM program.

insights.claim: The engineering work required to build competitive audio models is roughly a half to a third of the work of building the underlying language model — explicitly not a tenth — so public base models function only as a good prior rather than a shortcut.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Quantifies capital intensity for audio-model challengers: meaningfully cheaper than a frontier LLM but far from a fine-tuning-scale effort.
insights.quote: the work that's required in building the audio models is somewhat commensurate with the lang with the language model itself. Right? Maybe it's half or 1/3 uh but it's not one/10enth.

insights.claim: Bosan AI's base-model choice varies by product and is partly an economic decision — one model released last year was built on top of Llama with acknowledgment in the model card, while other models are proprietary or built in-house depending on required language performance.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Evidence that open-weight releases materially lower cost for downstream modality vendors, making open-weight availability a real input-cost variable for the sector.
insights.quote: one model that we released last year was built on top of llama and we acknowledge them appropriately in our model card

insights.claim: Audio understanding models are architecturally distinct from lightweight ASR: ASR converts audio to text without comprehension and cannot disambiguate homophones like 'recognize speech' versus 'wreck a nice beach', whereas an audio understanding model reasons over audio plus text prompts and reference audio.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: A clean taxonomy for evaluating speech vendors: commoditized ASR versus defensible audio-reasoning models sit in very different margin pools.

themes.theme: Two-stage agent architecture and MCP limits

insights.claim: Fully end-to-end audio models are responsive, small and low-latency but fundamentally dumb, and making them smart makes them unaffordable, so Bosan AI uses a two-stage architecture where understanding and reasoning happen in front while tool calls fire off in the background like threads off a main thread.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: The architecture choice is the cost strategy — expect voice vendors converging on orchestrated small-front-end designs rather than giant omni-models.

insights.claim: Bosan AI's models are prompted with the same look and feel as instructing a regular LLM, which lowers integration friction because customers do not have to relearn new techniques to adopt a voice model.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Prompt-interface compatibility is a real distribution advantage in enterprise voice; switching costs favor vendors that mimic existing LLM ergonomics.

insights.claim: The number of MCP servers that can be enabled simultaneously in Bosan AI's current voice system is limited by context window size and KV-cache-driven inference cost, with a next iteration promised to support significantly more.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: A concrete current constraint on voice-agent tool breadth: large prefill and KV cache directly raise per-token generation cost, capping integration surface area.
insights.quote: the quantity of servers at enabled at the same time right now is a little bit limited

insights.claim: Off-the-shelf MCP servers are both a feature and a necessity for voice agents — a necessity because neither the vendor nor its customers want to reinvent tooling, and a feature because it eases integration into existing systems — with nesting tool calls that themselves have MCP configured as the efficiency workaround.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Supports MCP becoming the default integration substrate even in latency-critical voice, rather than voice forcing bespoke high-speed tool protocols.

insights.claim: Slow tool latency in voice agents can be solved with user-experience design rather than engineering, because humans tolerate delays when told a delay is coming — the guest cites Apple's boot progress bar as a fake timer calibrated to the last boot duration, contrasted with Microsoft's truthful bar that sticks at 99%.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Reframes a hard latency problem as a cheap UX problem, meaning agent products can ship acceptable experiences without waiting for infrastructure speedups.
insights.quote: humans are very tolerant to delays is if they are told that there's a delay

insights.claim: Bosan AI's Higgs live demo performs web search in the background and dynamically chooses between answering immediately or verbally stalling depending on how fast the result returns, in order to preserve the illusion of an engaged conversational partner.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Adaptive stalling is an observable product capability to test when comparing voice agents — it is what makes tool-augmented voice feel usable.

insights.claim: The host reports that agentic systems built on off-the-shelf MCP servers are so slow that they are merely annoying in text but unimaginable in a voice scenario, raising the question of whether voice requires rebuilding the entire tool layer from the ground up.
insights.speaker: Sam Charrington (host)
insights.so_what: Flags latency of the tool/integration layer — not the model — as the practical bottleneck for shipping voice agents on existing infrastructure.

insights.claim: Optimization targets diverge sharply by domain: code-generation models optimize for task completion while voice models must optimize for human happiness, which the guest frames as the operational meaning of 'AI for humans'.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Implies voice-AI leaderboards will be won on different metrics than coding leaderboards, so cross-domain model rankings are poor predictors in this segment.
insights.quote: In our case, we worry about human happiness.

insights.claim: Interruptibility must be scene-dependent rather than uniform, because Japanese-style back-channeling acknowledgments should not stop the agent while a genuine 'I don't understand' should — a distinction the guest's Toronto team formalized in a benchmark called ProactBench, with a related benchmark called Ibench, published on arXiv about a month before the conversation.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Named, public benchmarks for conversational proactivity give buyers a way to evaluate voice agents beyond word error rate and latency.
insights.quote: So Proactbench is the one for productivity

insights.claim: Solving EQ from a text perspective does not transfer fully to voice — some interruptibility signals can be recovered from a transcript, but emotional appropriateness requires audio-native evaluation of whether the delivery matches what is being said.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Text-model EQ leadership does not automatically translate into voice-agent leadership, preserving room for audio-native specialists.
insights.quote: there is a difference between IQ and EQ

insights.claim: Movies, romantic comedies and talk shows are terrible reference data for training social behavior because the depicted conduct — stalking, violence followed by reconciliation — would result in arrest in reality, making naive entertainment corpora actively harmful for interaction training.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: A specific data-curation risk: the largest available corpora of human interaction are systematically unrepresentative of acceptable behavior.
insights.quote: I sincerely hope that nobody will train a model on Dr. Phil and assume that this is normal human behavior.

insights.claim: Third-party audio models are used inside Bosan AI's own benchmark definitions to measure interruptibility, responsiveness and whether delivered audio matches the intended content, making the evaluation reproducible rather than self-graded by the model under test.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Methodological detail worth verifying when assessing the vendor's benchmark claims — third-party judging is a credibility marker.

insights.claim: The guest frames voice as only an intermediate stepping stone toward audiovisual agents that look and feel human, and says the industry is still very far from making that natural.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Positions today's voice-agent leaders as holding a temporary rather than terminal position — the defensible endpoint is audiovisual.
insights.quote: I would argue that voice is an intermediate stepping stone.

insights.claim: The guest predicts audio AI becomes essentially bulletproof and ubiquitous within about one year, with avatar video feeds starting to appear in roughly a year to eighteen months and widely deployed on robots with fully animated faces.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: A dated roadmap to hold vendors to: audio commoditization in ~12 months implies margin compression in pure speech and value migration to avatars and robots.
insights.quote: I think probably in a year audio will become pretty much bulletproof.

insights.claim: Avatar deployment timelines run longer than software timelines because animated-head products require hardware, and Bosan AI is already working with a startup on the related problems.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Hardware lead times, not model capability, will gate the avatar-on-robot market — relevant to timing exposure to embodied-AI hardware suppliers.

insights.claim: Bosan AI trains against user simulators built on Nvidia's released digital personas and scenarios, deliberately including uncooperative, abrasive and adversarial users so models hold up against people trying to break the system.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Synthetic adversarial-persona training is becoming standard practice for conversational robustness, and Nvidia is supplying the raw personas for it.
insights.quote: Nvidia did a great job at releasing some digital personas and some scenarios and so on and we use that

insights.claim: The guest expects conversational AI improvement to split into two loops — personalized improvement from per-user memory that functions like a glorified CRM for everybody, and global behavioral improvement learned across all interactions — structurally resembling recommender systems.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: If voice agents inherit recommender-system dynamics, scale of interaction volume becomes the compounding moat — favoring whoever gets distribution first.

insights.claim: Cultural norms such as not eating with the left hand in India or not showing the soles of your feet in Thailand will drive region-specific personalization of agent behavior, adding a localization axis beyond language.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Cultural behavioral localization is an underappreciated product requirement and potential barrier to entry in global voice-agent deployments.

insights.claim: The guest argues that hand-crafted brilliance in human-interaction robotics is not repeatable or automatable, and the future lies in systems that automatically learn interaction skills from data so that brilliance is no longer required.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Predicts a shift in value from specialist research teams to data-and-scale operators in human-interaction AI.
insights.quote: Brilliance is good, but brilliance is not repeatable and automatable.

insights.claim: Skills most humans lack — like a teacher keeping composure with uncooperative children or delivering critique via the praise-critique-praise sandwich — can still be learned by agents through interaction data and exploration, resolving the objection that absent behaviors cannot be in the training set.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: Implies live interaction data, not static corpora, becomes the scarce asset for building emotionally competent agents.

insights.claim: The guest expects the shift toward agents that learn human interaction from data to be a fast-moving revolution over the next two to three years.
insights.speaker: Alex Mhola (guest, co-founder & CEO, Bosan AI)
insights.so_what: A concrete two-to-three-year horizon for when emotionally adaptive agents move from research to deployed products.
insights.quote: This is this is I think really going to be quite the an exciting revolution for the next maybe two to three years.
